# The data

The same file as in Ex-8-1. `data/8-1-county-crops.csv` has one row per county and year, for counties in Colorado, Kansas and Nebraska, 2000 to 2018. Source: USDA NASS county yields and the US Drought Monitor.

| Column | What it is |
|---|---|
| `state_name`, `county_code`, `county_name` | The county |
| `year` | The year |
| `corn_yield` | Corn yield (bushels per acre) |
| `soy_yield` | Soybean yield (bushels per acre) |
| `weeks_severe` | Weeks from May to September in severe drought (US Drought Monitor category D2) |
| `weeks_extreme` | Weeks from May to September in extreme or exceptional drought (categories D3 and D4) |

The question: how much lower are corn and soybean yields for each additional week of drought? The models, one per column of the table:

1. corn yield on weeks of severe drought and weeks of extreme drought
2. soybean yield on weeks of severe drought and weeks of extreme drought

# Task 3: The regression table

**My request to the AI.** Fill in every `<...>` from Task 2:

```text
In my R project, the table crops has one row per county and year. The
columns used: corn_yield and soy_yield (bushels per acre; soy_yield is
missing on <...> rows), weeks_severe and weeks_extreme (weeks from May
to September in severe drought and in extreme or exceptional drought).

Estimate linear regressions, one per column, in this order: (1)
corn_yield on weeks_severe and weeks_extreme; (2) soy_yield on
weeks_severe and weeks_extreme. The
message is about the weeks_extreme estimate, and how it differs between
corn and soybeans. Use robust standard errors (HC1). Show the rows
weeks_extreme, weeks_severe and the constant, in that order, and at the
bottom only the number of observations. Use modelsummary.

Check: each column's header next to its model's formula; the number of
observations of each model (I expect <...> and <...>); and every
coefficient of each model against the rows of the table.

Every table must meet this standard:
1. Column headers and row labels in plain words with units, such as
   "Corn yield (bushels per acre)", never a column name such as
   corn_yield.
2. Categories in words, such as "Irrigated", never a code such as 1.
3. Numbers rounded to what the message needs, with the same number of
   decimals down each column.
4. Thousands separators in large numbers, except in years.
5. Percentages shown as percentages.
6. Numbers right-aligned so that the digits line up; text left-aligned.
7. Text no smaller than the document's body text.
8. Fits the page width where it will appear, without scrolling.
9. Rows in an order that serves the message (by value, or in time
   order), not alphabetical unless the reader will search a long table.
10. A title that says what the numbers are.
11. A note giving the source of the data.
12. A note saying how any computed column was computed.
13. The number of observations behind each value, when it varies.
14. Nothing the message does not need: no extra columns, no row
    numbers, no heavy borders, no colours that only decorate.
For regression tables, also:
15. One column per model, with headers or a title saying what each
    model explains.
16. Standard errors in parentheses below each estimate, with their kind
    stated in a note.
17. Significance stars left out, or defined in a note and used the same
    way in every table.
18. The number of observations for every model.

plain-English sentence saying what it does and why. Build every path

its own line as "name of check: expected X, got Y". Render the document
```

# Task 5: Read someone else's AI code

First, with a neighbour and **without** the AI or running anything. Alex asked an AI to "compare the effect of drought on corn and soybeans, with robust standard errors" and kept this:

```{r}
#| label: task-5
#| eval: false
crops <- read_csv(here::here("data", "8-1-county-crops.csv")) |>
  na.omit()
corn <- lm(corn_yield ~ weeks_severe + weeks_extreme, data = crops)
soy <- lm(soy_yield ~ weeks_severe + weeks_extreme, data = crops)
modelsummary(
  list("Corn" = corn, "Soybeans" = soy),
  vcov = "HC1",
  coef_map = c("weeks_extreme" = "Weeks of extreme drought")
)
```

**A. In plain words, what does each line do? (`na.omit()` removes every row that has a missing value in any column.)**
